evidence.excerpt: Agritourism properties in Vojvodina operate under capacity constraints far tighter than urban hotels and serve communities where visible price discrimination may carry social costs. This book chapter synthesises 14 semi-structured interviews with agritourism operators and a discrete-choice experiment with 380 potential guests to assess the acceptability and revenue potential of demand-responsive pricing in this segment. Interview analysis identifies three adoption barriers: lack of forecasting skills, fear of negative word-of-mouth, and perceived incompatibility with the 'authentic rural' brand. The discrete-choice experiment shows that guests tolerate price premiums of up to 18% during peak agritourism weekends but penalise perceived arbitrariness by switching to competitors at premiums above 25%. The chapter concludes with a practical tiered pricing framework calibrated to these tolerance thresholds and compatible with simple spreadsheet management.
